name: way-Motion Construction

dimensions.form: VP headed by make or a manner-denoting verb, followed by the direct-object NP x's way and a change-of-location PP complement, centrally bearing a path, goal, or direction role
dimensions.meaning: The participant identified by x progresses along a route, in a direction, or toward a goal by the activity or means expressed by the verb
dimensions.function: The fixed way-object frame licenses a change-of-location complement and allows the verb to specify the manner or means of progress
dimensions.distribution: VP-internal; found in the make one's way idiom and a productive extension with manner or means verbs

1.definition: A participant progresses along the path, in the direction, or toward the goal expressed by the locative complement
1.details: CGEL analyzes x's way as an Od, not as a preposition or as part of the following PP. Make one's way is an idiom meaning approximately 'progress' that licenses change-of-location complements although make alone does not do so. This idiom provides the basis for a productive construction in which another verb supplies the manner or means of progress (CGEL Ch. 8 §4.3, p. 685; Ch. 4 §8.1.3, p. 305).

examples.form: We [made our way to the station].
examples.note: Make one's way idiom with a goal-role locative complement

examples.form: Jill had to [elbow her way to the exit].
examples.note: Productive manner/means verb; the frame supplies progress toward the goal

examples.form: They [pushed their way to the front].
examples.note: Way Od precedes a goal-role locative complement

constraints.description: The fixed-form NP x's way is Od of the verb; the following PP is a separate change-of-location Comp:PP, centrally bearing a path, goal, or direction role.
The way NP contains a genitive determiner form and way as nominal head; the genitive identifies the participant whose progress is described.
Make licenses the frame idiomatically; productive alternatives contribute the manner or means by which progress is achieved.
The VP denotes directed progress along a route, in a direction, or toward a goal rather than ordinary creation or possession of a way referent.
In CGEL's account, the movement consists of a series of stops and starts rather than uninterrupted continuous motion.

projection.target: The fixed x's way Od followed by a change-of-location complement predicts a progress interpretation, constructional licensing of path, goal, or direction with non-motion manner verbs, and interpretation of the verb as the manner or means of progress rather than as selecting an ordinary way object
projection.evidence: CGEL relates the make one's way idiom to productive manner/means replacements such as elbow and push, while retaining Od and locative-complement functions (Ch. 8 §4.3, p. 685; Ch. 4 §8.1.3, p. 305).

core.property: Manner or means supplied by Head:V

known_boundary_items: made a way through the wall: ordinary creation of a path-denoting object lacks the fixed genitive way-object profile
caused motion: its Od denotes the moving theme, whereas the way construction's Od is the fixed x's way NP
An ordinary goal-complement VP lacks the construction-specific way object

relatedConstructions.notes: The fixed x's way constituent is an NP functioning as Od
Non-pronominal x's way NPs realize the determiner through the genitive-s construction
The route, direction, or endpoint is expressed by a locative PP complement
The final locative complement can express the route traversed
The final locative complement can express the endpoint of progress
Both combine manner or means with motion, but they assign different functions and roles to Od

grounds.note: x's way is Od and the following change-of-location dependent is a locative complement
Fixed way object, productive manner-verb replacement, and locative licensing form a recurrent profile

curious.title: Making your way somewhere
curious.summary: Phrases like "elbowed her way to the exit" say how someone moved forward and where they were heading.
curious.body: We made our way to the station. Jill had to elbow her way to the exit. They pushed their way to the front. In each, the person makes progress toward a place. In the last two, the verb (elbow, push) says how they managed it. The pattern needs a word like our, her or their, plus way, followed by a phrase saying where. It isn't about a way that someone builds or owns. It describes getting forward along a route, in a direction or toward a goal. On the account this dictionary follows, the movement goes in a series of stops and starts, not in one smooth motion.

examples.text: We [made our way to the station].
Jill had to [elbow her way to the exit].
They [pushed their way to the front].

curious.try: Replace elbowed with another action, such as squeezed or fought, in She elbowed her way to the exit. Does the sentence still say she was making progress toward the exit?

teacher.summary: Explains how verbs like push can describe progress toward a place when followed by x's way and a locative phrase.
teacher.explain: In We made our way to the station, make one's way is an idiom meaning roughly "progress". It licenses a change-of-location complement even though make alone doesn't. A productive extension replaces make with a verb of manner or means (elbow, push), which then says how the progress is achieved. In CGEL's analysis, x's way is the direct object, not part of the preposition phrase. The genitive determiner (her, their, Kim's) identifies the person making progress, and way is the head. The following PP is a separate locative complement giving the path, goal or direction. In CGEL's account, the movement is a series of stops and starts.
teacher.terms: Direct object (Od): x's way. Complement (Comp): the PP of path, goal or direction. Genitive: the form identifying whose way, such as her or Kim's.

examples.text: We [made our way to the station].
Jill had to [elbow her way to the exit].
They [pushed their way to the front].

contrasts.text: They pushed their way to the front.
contrasts.note: The way phrase is the object, and the PP says where.

contrasts.text: They made a way through the wall.
contrasts.note: Ordinary creation of a path, without the fixed genitive way-object.

watch_for: A learner might read their way as an ordinary object naming a route someone owns.
A learner might take the PP as part of the way phrase rather than as a separate complement.
A learner might read pushed their way to the front as pushing the way itself, rather than pushing in order to move forward.
teacher.activity: Give students a destination (the exit, the front, the station) and cards with verbs (push, fight, make). They build sentences with a person's own way and a phrase of place, then discuss how each verb changes the picture of getting there.

child.hook: When you squeeze through a crowd, how would you say it with the word "way"?
child.explain: Some sentences use someone's own way to show them making progress toward a place. He pushed his way to the front. Here pushed tells how he moved, and the last part tells where he was going.

examples.text: We [made our way to the station].
He [elbowed his way to the door].
They [pushed their way to the front].

child.play: Pick a place, like the door or the front. Then say how you'd get there with your way, using words like pushed, squeezed or made.

Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'.
